props.title: Ninja III: The Domination

sections.content: Ninja III: The Domination represents peak 1980s Cannon Films absurdity, blending supernatural possession, ninja action, and aerobics in a gloriously bizarre cocktail. Following the success of Enter the Ninja (1981) and Revenge of the Ninja (1983), Cannon pushed the genre into supernatural territory, creating what's essentially The Exorcist meets American Ninja. Director Sam Firstenberg, who helmed several Cannon classics including American Ninja (1985), embraces the film's outlandish premise with complete sincerity, resulting in unforgettable scenes like a possessed aerobics instructor dispatching police officers with ninja skills.

sections.content: The ninja boom of the 1980s spawned dozens of imitators trying to capitalize on the craze. The Master (1984) with Lee Van Cleef attempted a ninja TV series, while Miami Connection (1987) merged ninja action with new wave rock bands. But none matched the sheer audacity of Ninja III's genre-bending approach. The film's use of arcade games, V8 juice, and ninja possession creates an unintentionally hilarious time capsule of 1984 pop culture, elevated by Lucinda Dickey's committed performance and Sho Kosugi's authentic martial arts expertise.

The film's practical effects, while dated, showcase the creative ambition of low-budget 1980s filmmaking. Smoke bombs, practical wire work, and hand-crafted props create a tangible world that CGI-heavy modern ninja films like Ninja Assassin (2009) often lack. The possession scenes, complete with glowing eyes and levitating swords, draw clear inspiration from The Exorcist (1973) while adding distinctly Eastern martial arts elements. sections.content: While Ninja III: The Domination marked the end of Cannon's original ninja trilogy, its influence echoed through the decade. The film's success helped greenlight more martial arts features like American Ninja (1985) and its four sequels. Modern filmmakers like Robert Rodriguez and Quentin Tarantino have cited these Cannon productions as influential to their own style, with Rodriguez's Planet Terror (2007) specifically paying homage to the era's genre-blending approach.
